paper_title: HybridResearcher: Bridging the Structured-Unstructured Boundary for Deep Research Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: While LLM agents are increasingly capable of gathering and synthesizing evidence from a single homogeneous source, such as structured tables or unstructured data, real-world analytical questions frequently span heterogeneous sources. For example, answering one enterprise question may require both a result computed over an internal database and evidence found on the web. Recent evaluations on benchmarks like HybridDeepResearch show that even frontier agents struggle when evidence must cross this boundary. While these benchmarks have exposed the limitation, methodologies to explicitly teach cross-source reasoning remain absent. To address this, we introduce HybridResearcher, a 4B agent trained to bridge evidence across the structured and unstructured boundary. To build it, we synthesize cross-source bridge trajectories by starting with validated single-source tasks-such as existing text-to-SQL or web search queries-and fabricating the missing source around a bridge entity drawn from the seed's own output. We retain a sample only when strict construction gates confirm that neither side alone suffices, ensuring the data requires true cross-source interdependence. Finally, we train on this curated dataset using supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. Evaluated on the existing HybridDeepResearch benchmark, HybridResearcher improves over our base model, Qwen3.5-4B, by 30.0 points pass@8 and surpasses the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B by 8.3 points, while also improving over its base model on established, held-out single-source benchmarks (BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus), demonstrating that this complex cross-source reasoning can be taught directly to small models without triggering catastrophic forgetting.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: LLM agents extend language models beyond closed-form reasoning by letting them interact with external data sources through tools (Yao et al., 2023; Schick et al., 2023). capable agent can write and execute SQL against database, navigate the open web to locate and synthesize evidence, or query domain-specific APIs to retrieve information that parametric knowledge alone cannot supply. Training agents for these capabilities has advanced rapidly: recent recipes that combine synthetic data construction, supervised fine-tuning, and reinforcement learning have produced compact models that rival or surpass frontier models, in domains such as text-to-SQL (Li et al., 2025a; Yao et al., 2026), and open-web deep research (Jin et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025; Xie et al., 2026). However, these recipes typically operate within single homogeneous source, such as database or the web, rarely bridging both in the same reasoning chain. Real-world analytical tasks rarely observe this boundary: domains routinely require synthesizing evidence across structured and unstructured sources to answer single questionsuch as crossing internal transaction databases with public Equal contribution. SEC filings for financial auditing, or merging inventory SQL with global news for supply-chain risk assessment (Abaskohi et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2026b). Recent benchmarks such as HybridDeepResearch (Wu et al., 2026b) make this gap measurable, revealing that even frontier agents such as GPT-5 (OpenAI, 2025) and Claude-Sonnet-4.6 (Anthropic, 2026) struggle to synthesize answers when evidence must cross this boundary. Yet while the evaluation gap is now visible, the training gap remains: to our knowledge, no prior work provides training framework, training data, or trained model for agents that must bridge structured and unstructured sources within single reasoning chain. To address this training gap, we ask: why does this capability gap persist despite rapid progress on each source in isolation? We identify two core obstacles. First, component capabilities do not automatically compose into hybrid reasoning. Fine-tuning model on single-source corpora (whether SQL-only, search-only, or their union) without bridged trajectories fails to yield crosssource competence. While the union model almost fully recovers parallel tasks that exercise both skills independently, performance on genuinely directional tasks, where the output of one source conditions the other, remains severely impaired. This demonstrates that hybrid data must explicitly teach the bridge itself: the interdependent execution between sources rather than the isolated skills. Second, naive hybrid synthesis is vulnerable to shortcut learning. Among teacher trajectories accepted by standard correctness filters, 79.5% never execute substantive SQL query. Instead, the model answers directly from parametric memory, bypassing the cross-source hop entirely. model trained on such flawed trajectories merely learns to fake the bridge, failure mode that scaling uncurated data only exacerbates. Overcoming both obstacles by explicitly teaching the cross-source bridge while enforcing strict anti-shortcut guarantees forms the foundation of our methodology. We introduce HYBRIDRESEARCHER, training framework that teaches hybrid deep research to small models, by extending validated single-source tasks across the structured/unstructured boundary. The core idea is that hybrid training data need not be fabricated from scratch. Each instance starts from seed whose difficulty is already establishedan existing text-to-SQL task or websearch task. We synthesize the missing source around bridge entity drawn from the seeds own output, so that the seeds difficulty is inherited rather than re-established. To directly address the shortcut problem, we retain an instance only when strict construction gates deterministically verify that neither source alone suffices, ensuring the bridge entity forms the unique, necessary path between them (examples in Appendix C.4 and D.3). While we instantiate this framework for the SQLweb pairing, the structural reciperequiring only validated single-source task to seed from and an entity that can bridge across boundariesprovides clear blueprint for extending agentic reasoning to other heterogeneous combinations in the future. The curated data serves both supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, trained in reproducible offline environment built around frozen corpus and local retriever. To optimize this complex policy, our RL recipe introduces majority-voting judge ensemble to mitigate reward noise, alongside strict hard-gating mechanisms that terminate and penalize degenerate, brute-force tool usage. Figure 1 summarizes this pipeline. Evaluated on the HybridDeepResearch benchmark (Wu et al., 2026b), HYBRIDRESEARCHER-4B improves over its Qwen3.5-4B (Qwen Team, 2026a) base model by 30.0 points pass@8 and sur2 passes the far larger Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 by 8.3 points. Crucially, this improvement does not come at the cost of single-source ability: HYBRIDRESEARCHER-4B also outperforms its base model on the held-out SQL-only benchmark Spider 2.0-lite (Lei et al., 2025) and on the web-search benchmarks BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) and BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2026). By explicitly teaching the cross-source bridge, our framework successfully imparts advanced hybrid reasoning capabilities to compact model without triggering catastrophic forgetting (Luo et al., 2025).

sections.title: 2 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Single-source Agents. Tool-using LLM agents have made rapid progress on tasks that draw evidence from one type of source. For databases, benchmarks have moved from single-turn semantic parsing (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023) to realistic workflows over large enterprise schemas (Lei et al., 2025; BIRD Team, 2025), and agents now explore the database and revise their queries based on execution results (Deng et al., 2025). Small models trained on synthetic data (Li et al., 2025a) or with reinforcement learning from execution rewards (Ma et al., 2025; Yao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025) are now competitive with much larger models on these benchmarks. For the web, search agents interleave reasoning with retrieval (Yao et al., 2023; Jin et al., 2025; Song et al., 2025; Zheng et al., 2025), and recent systems can answer long-horizon questions whose answers are hard to find, as measured by BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025). These systems are trained largely on synthetic tasks designed to be hard, for example by obscuring key entities (Li et al., 2025b), formalizing the structure of information-seeking tasks (Tao et al., 2026), sampling paths from knowledge graphs (Lu et al., 2025), or generating fully synthetic research tasks (Xie et al., 2026), and then refined with reinforcement learning (Gao et al., 2025). However, in all of these works, the agents work with single source. In contrast, we train an agent that crosses the boundary between structured and unstructured sources, carrying evidence found in one source into its search of the other. Reasoning across Heterogeneous Sources. Hybrid question answering has long studied questions that require both tables and text (Chen et al., 2020; 2021a;b; Zhu et al., 2021), but the evidence is either given or retrieved in one step, and the model neither executes queries nor decides which source to consult next. Other work adds language-model reasoning to database queries (Liu et al., 2024). Recent benchmarks evaluate agents that combine evidence from heterogeneous sources, including databases and documents (Wang et al., 2026b; Ma et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), enterprise files and the web (Abaskohi et al., 2026), web pages and knowledge-graph APIs (Yang et al., 2024), databases and web search (Wu et al., 2026b), and multimodal evidence on the web (Wang et al., 2026a). These benchmarks measure how well agents combine sources, but few works train agents to do so. DSLR1 (Hu et al., 2026) merges structured filters and vector search into single query language over closed collection, so the agent never has to carry result from one kind of source to another. Wu et al. (2026a) synthesize simple two-hop questions that pair SQL query with single Wikipedia passage lookup, and train agents with hint-guided reinforcement learning. We instead present full training recipefrom data construction to supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learningfor significantly more challenging, multi-hop questions that combine hard SQL execution with longhorizon web search.

sections.title: 3 METHODOLOGY: SYNTHESIZING CROSS-SOURCE TRAJECTORIES
sections.content: To train agents for hybrid reasoning, we require trajectories that exhibit true cross-source interdependence. Training on existing single-source data does not produce this capability, and synthesizing hybrid data naively invites shortcuts (3.1). We therefore build hybrid trajectories from validated single-source seeds, starting from either text-to-SQL tasks (3.2) or search tasks (3.3).

sections.title: 3.1 TWO OBSTACLES TO TRAINING HYBRID AGENTS
sections.content: Single-Source Data Does Not Teach Hybrid Capability. Text-to-SQL (Yu et al., 2018; Li et al., 2023) and web search (Du et al., 2026; Chu et al., 2026) training data are available in large quantities, whereas hybrid trajectories have to be synthesized. We therefore first test whether single-source data alone is enough. We fine-tune Qwen3.5-4B on successful trajectories from text-to-SQL tasks only, web-search tasks only, or their union, and evaluate on the hard subset of HybridDeepResearch (Wu 3 Figure 2: Overview of sql-originated data construction.Top (SQL2S): an output cell (Northstar) that passes the membership gate, entity-quality gate, and judge check becomes the bridge; coined facts about it (HQ city ...) become search constraints that only one hub, Velora Labs, satisfies. Bottom (S2SQL): WHERE literal from the SQL AST (Oslo) that passes the membership gate and execution check becomes the anchor, and the answer is the unchanged SQL output. Gold and hard-negative documents for every clue are inserted with real web text by the retriever used at evaluation. (Details: 3.2 and Appendix C) et al., 2026b), whose 120 questions each require both SQL and web search. None of the three mixtures helps. SQL-only training reaches 31.67 pass@8, within one question of the base models 30.83, while union and search-only training fall to 29.17 and 15.83. Single-source trajectories never use the output of one tool as the input to the other, so training on them does not teach this step. Naive Hybrid Synthesis Invites Shortcuts. Synthesizing hybrid questions and keeping the teacher trajectories that reach the correct answer is also not enough, because correct answer does not show that both sources were used. When the facts on the search side are well known, the teacher can recall them instead of searching, and when the question reveals the bridge entity, the teacher can skip the hop that was meant to produce it. Models tend to trust such parametric knowledge even when it conflicts with retrieved evidence (Xie et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). This risk is concrete in our setting. Bridge entities drawn from real databases are often famous, and the models prior can override what it retrieves. Such trajectories lead the model to answer without crossing the boundary.

sections.title: 3.2 SQL-ORIGINATED TRAJECTORIES
sections.content: We construct hybrid tasks from complete text-to-SQL seeds by deriving multi-constraint webretrieval subtask from seed entity (Figure 2, Appendix C). Building SQL2S. (i) Bridge Selection: We select cell from the executed output table to serve as the bridge entity (e.g., Northstar in Figure 2). membership gate ensures this cell appears in the output but not in the original question, deterministically forcing the agent to execute the SQL query to discover it. (ii) Hop One (Coined Facts): To prevent the model from bypassing the tool boundary via parametric memory, we invent novel facts (e.g., business rules) about the bridge entity using pronounceable pseudo-words. Each fact is paired with fabricated gold document and typed hard negatives that perturb exactly one constraint. (iii) Hop Two (The Intersection Hub): The solver must resolve the bridge by SQL, resolve each coined fact by search, and find the single hub that all facts point to (e.g., Velora Labs). The gold hub satisfies all constraints, while each near-miss distractor satisfies exactly 1, forcing rigorous multi-document cross-referencing. (iv) Verification: The item must pass deterministic gates (e.g., ensuring the constraint intersection is singleton) and model-based checks, including mask test proving the answer cannot be guessed from negative documents. Building S2SQL. (i) Anchor Selection: We select string literal from an equality, inclusion, or pattern-matching predicate in the gold SQL query to serve as the anchor (Appendix C.4, Oslo in Figure 2). An execution test requires that removing the predicate changes the result, and membership constraints require the literal to occur in the original question but not in the output. Together, these checks verify the anchor is load-bearing: the agent must resolve it via web search. (ii) Relation Fan4 Figure 3: The search-originated pipeline. One hard-search item yields SQL2S or S2SQL according to whether the bridge is taken from the question or the answer. Both directions share the same stages: plan, improve, build, bridge, and final improve, and draw SQL difficulty from catalog of executable patterns. out & Hub Construction: We coin multiple distinctive entities related to the anchor. The anchor is hidden in the final question and replaced with intersecting search clues. The agent is strictly forced to resolve these clues on the web to identify the anchor before it can formulate the correct SQL query.

sections.title: 3.3 SEARCH-ORIGINATED TRAJECTORIES
sections.content: We construct hybrid tasks from hard-search seeds by adding synthetic text-to-SQL component around seed entity (Figure 3, Appendix D). The original seed supplies the web-retrieval requirement; the constructed database supplies the independently nontrivial SQL requirement. single search item can support both directions (SQL2S, S2SQL) depending on which text span is selected as the bridge. SQL2S: The bridge is an entity mentioned in the original search question (e.g., Qujing in Figure 3). We formulate SQL task where this entity is the answer. The agent is forced to query the database to discover the entity before it can complete the web search. S2SQL: The bridge is the search answer itself (e.g., 1994). This value becomes required parameter that the SQL query consumes. The agent must successfully resolve the web search to find this parameter before executing the database query. Construction Pipeline. Both directions run through multi-stage generation pipeline to ensure the fabricated database requires genuine structured reasoning, preventing it from degrading into trivial lookup table: (i) Plan: We select advanced SQL techniques from catalog of executable patterns (e.g., grouped aggregation, ranking) and design schema containing only raw observational data (e.g., individual event records rather than precomputed yearly stats). (ii) Improve: The schema is refined to strictly eliminate any columns that might pre-aggregate the answer, logically guaranteeing the gold query cannot be simplified by shortcut logic. (iii) Build: The planned schema is materialized into populated SQLite database. To prevent trivial edge-case filtering, we dynamically generate same-kind peer entities and bury the target entity deeply within the data distribution. (iv) Bridge & Final Improve: The original search clues and the newly fabricated SQL constraints are merged into single cohesive prompt. The bridge entity is completely masked, and scope hints are added only to resolve genuine ambiguities. Load-Bearing Verification. To guarantee interdependence, both hops must pass strict execution checks. For SQL2S, the bridge must never appear in the merged question text. For S2SQL, the bridge must not leak into the final SQL result table. Crucially, the fabricated database must present structurally fresh query rather than merely mirroring the search clues; otherwise, the SQL tool acts as trivial lookup cache for web puzzle the agent has already solved.

sections.title: 4.1 SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING
sections.content: Trajectory generation. Our SFT mixture combines directly used training data (Appendix B) with judge-correct trajectories generated by running the agent harness (Appendix G) against the local corpus (Appendix F) and databases. We use either Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (Qwen Team, 2026a) or DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeek-AI, 2026) for generating trajectories. We set temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20, thinking on, 3600 timeout, with 32k max tokens set to SQL-originated tasks and 128k for search-originated tasks. Max turns range from 100 to 300 depending on the task.

sections.title: 4.2 REINFORCEMENT LEARNING
sections.content: Data Curation. We collect 21K synthesized hybrid tasks that remained unsolved during the SFT stage as candidates for RL. Because RL is highly sensitive to noisy data (Ye et al., 2026; Tang et al., 2026), we aggressively filter this pool down to 0.7K high-signal QA pairs using strict three-stage pipeline. (i) Difficulty filtering: we execute preliminary rollouts and discard tasks that are either consistently solved (too easy) or never solved (too hard or unsolvable), ensuring the dataset targets the exact frontier of the models capabilities. (ii) Quality filtering: data-quality agent removes QA pairs with ambiguous answers, duplicate search chains, or inconsistent cross-source evidence. We actively prioritize questions requiring broad multi-hop retrieval or complex SQL operations. (iii) Distribution balancing: to prevent policy collapse on single source or task family, we strictly balance the final 0.7K dataset 1:1 between SQL-originated and search-originated tasks, and 1:1 between the S2SQL and SQL2S directions. RL recipe. Our RL training is based on CISPO (MiniMax et al., 2025), with several techniques introduced to improve training efficiency and stability. Further details are provided in Appendix J.1. Hard-gating: As invalid tool interactions and malformed tool calls will introduce noisy or substantial variance training signals into policy optimization, we applied strict hard-gating rules to increase training and tool-use efficiency: rollout is terminated early and assigned zero reward when it exhausts the turn budget without making tool call, contains malformed tool arguments, invokes nonexistent tools, fails to produce valid final answer, or repeatedly issues duplicated tool queries. Judge majority-voting: RL is highly sensitive to noisy reward signals. Relying on single LLM judge frequently produces unreliable evaluations, particularly when correctness requires nuanced semantic matching (e.g., distinguishing Charles III from Charles Emmanuel III) or recognizing semantically equivalent SQL solutions that differ in surface-level table form. To stabilize optimization, both S2SQL and SQL2S use an LLM-as-a-judge with five-vote majority to determine the binary pass/fail reward. An empirical analysis of this voting mechanism is presented in 6.3.

BrowseComp is evaluated against the live web, whereas BrowseComp-Plus uses its fixed corpus of 100,195 documents, providing complementary evaluation under dynamic and static retrieval environments. sections.title: 5.1 RESULTS
sections.content: Hybrid training progressively unlocks cross-source reasoning. As shown in Table 1, the Qwen3.5-4B base model fundamentally struggles with cross-source tasks, achieving only 30.83% overall pass@8. Our hybrid SFT framework successfully bridges this gap, nearly doubling the performance to 59.17%. Applying RL yields further gains, particularly in the avg@8 metric (increasing from 23.75% to 27.19% overall). This improvement highlights that RL makes the model more confident and consistent in arriving at the correct answer, primarily by strengthening the strictly interdependent directional tasks (e.g., S2SQL avg@8 increases from 26.88% to 31.56%). Remarkably, despite its small size, our final 4B agent approaches the performance of substantially larger frontier models like Claude Sonnet 4.6 (65.83% pass@8), GLM-5.2-FP4 (GLM-5-Team et al., 2026) (63.33% pass@8) and decisively surpasses its own familys flagship, Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-FP8 (52.50% pass@8 and 26.77% avg@8), on both metrics. Hybrid training preserves and improves single-source capabilities. Fine-tuning compact model on complex new behaviors frequently risks catastrophic forgetting of component skills. However, Table 2 demonstrates that HYBRIDRESEARCHER-4B entirely avoids this tradeoff. Instead of cannibalizing existing knowledge, hybrid SFT actually creates synergistic effect, substantially improving the base models standalone capabilities. On the search side, BrowseComp pass@8 increases from 54.03% to 61.37%, and BrowseComp-Plus from 60.84% to 69.76%. On the SQL side, Spider 2.0-lite execution accuracy jumps from 59.26% to 65.19%. Applying hybrid RL largely preserves these single-source improvements (e.g., further boosting BrowseComp-Plus to 73.13% pass@8). sections.title: 6.1 BEHAVIORAL SHIFTS: HOW SFT AND RL TRANSFORM TOOL USE
sections.content: To understand how our training recipe builds hybrid capability, we analyze the agents search behavior on the evaluation set (Tables 3 and 4). SFT teaches structured exploration. The base model exhibits naive search policy, firing off many queries (38.6 per rollout) but rarely reading the results (0.29 page visits per search). SFT corrects this imbalance. The agent learns to systematically explore retrieved content, nearly halving the number of web searches while significantly increasing page visits. This transition from blind searching to active reading improves basic evidence extraction, raising SQL2S accuracy (when the gold answer is present) from 12.9% to 18.5%. RL optimizes for precision and evidence utilization. While SFT teaches the basic mechanics, RL concentrates the policy on its successful behaviors. After RL, the agents search behavior becomes highly deliberate: queries become longer, more specific (48.8% use quotes, and operator use doubles), and far less redundant (exact repeats drop by 63%). Consequently, the agent extracts evidence effectively; on SQL2S, the agents ability to capitalize on surfaced gold answers jumps from 18.5% to 27.2%. Crucially, RL achieves these gains without inflating the trajectory cost, maintaining similar or less turn counts and token usage to the SFT checkpoint. Remaining Bottlenecks. Despite these improvements, cross-source reasoning remains bottlenecked by retrieval limits and early stopping. On S2SQL, the required bridge entity still fails to surface in 22.2% of rollouts. Moreover, 82.0% of RLs wrong answers (vs. 48.7% of its correct ones) cites time budget, the effort already spent, or guess (Appendix I.2), suggesting they commit under self-acknowledged uncertainty. Making the decision to search more when uncertain and refraining from guessing could be promising next direction.

sections.title: 6.2 DATA QUALITY OUTWEIGHS SCALE IN RL OPTIMIZATION
sections.content: To demonstrate that RL benefits more from high-signal data than sheer volume, we compare our curated RL dataset against the full 21K candidate pool using the identical training recipe. Despite being fraction of the size, the curated dataset achieves 27.2% overall avg@8, substantially outperforming the massive unfiltered pool (21.0%). This performance gap is driven by training efficiency: in the curated dataset, 71% of rollout groups provide sufficient reward contrast to contribute to policy updates, compared to just 38% in the uncurated pool. This confirms that aggressive filtering prevents noisy or uninformative trajectories from diluting the RL optimization process, making data curation much stronger lever than scaling data volume. 8 Figure 4: Training rollout length (left), tool calls per rollout (middle) and the share of rollouts with duplicated tool calls (right), with and without hard gating. Hard gating helps suppress redundant tool calls and stabilize rollout length. 6.3 JUDGE MAJORITY-VOTING HELPS IMPROVE REWARD RELIABILITY To quantify the impact of the majority judging ensemble introduced in Section 4.2, we compare it against single-vote baseline. The five-vote mechanism improves the models overall avg@8 from 25.2% to 27.2%. Telemetry from our training rollouts reveals exactly why this stabilization is necessary: single judges verdict disagrees with the final consensus in 8.2% of cases. This instability is heavily concentrated in the S2SQL direction (12.2% disagreement, compared to just 1.2% for SQL2S), confirming that evaluating executable logic combined with complex web entities is highly variance-prone. By smoothing out these individual judge errors (examples in Appendix J.2), majority voting successfully prevents noisy rewards from degrading the policy.

sections.title: 6.4 HARD-GATING YIELDS CLEANER TRAINING SIGNAL AND EFFICIENT TOOL-USE
sections.content: Hard-gating termination substantially improves both performance and rollout efficiency. Removing the hard-gating rules lowers avg@8 from 27.2% to 25.6%. We attribute this degradation to positive feedback loop in tool use: without hard gating, redundant or invalid actions are insufficiently penalized, causing the policy to increasingly favor prolonged trajectories and redundant tool calls. As shown in Figure 4, both trajectory token length and tool-call counts increase throughout training without hard gating, while remaining stable with hard gating. This trend also carries over to evaluation: hard gating reduces average tool calls from 76 to 55 per question and repeated-call frequency from 49% to 11%. The fraction of questions failing to produce valid answer also drops from 10.7% to 0.0%. Overall, hard gating suppresses inefficient tool use and provides cleaner training signals, leading to more efficient and reliable tool use, consistent with the observations in 6.1.

sections.title: 7 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We studied how to train agents for questions that require evidence from both structured database and unstructured web text, where result obtained from one source must be carried into the other. Training on existing single-source data does not produce this capability, and synthesizing hybrid data naively invites shortcuts. We therefore build training data by extending validated text-to-SQL and deep-search tasks across the boundary, keep only instances that construction gates confirm require both sources, and train on them with supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning. HYBRIDRESEARCHER-4B improves over its base model by 30.00 points pass@8 on HybridDeepResearch and outperforms Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, while also improving on single-source SQL and search benchmarks. Our analysis shows that fine-tuning teaches the agent to read what it retrieves instead of issuing many searches, and that reinforcement learning benefits more from small curated task set than from larger unfiltered pool. More broadly, this work provides complete training recipe for agents that reason across heterogeneous sources, and we hope it can be carried over to real-world settings that combine other kinds of sources, such as internal documents, code repositories, or domain-specific databases.

sections.title: AI USE STATEMENT
sections.content: Required disclosures. Generative AI is part of our method, so we disclose several required uses. (i) Generating synthetic datasets. The training data of 3 were synthesized with LLMs, but every item starts from real seed (a text-to-SQL query or web-search question). SFT trajectories were sampled from teacher models. (ii) Cleaning and filtering datasets. LLM judges scored candidate entities, checked data quality, and ran the model-based verification gates, alongside deterministic, non-LLM gates. (iii) Evaluation. HybridDeepResearch, BrowseComp, and BrowseComp-Plus answers were graded by an LLM judge (Qwen3.8-27B, majority of five votes); Spider 2.0-lite uses its deterministic execution-accuracy metric. sections.title: A OVERVIEW
sections.content: This appendix provides the data-construction details, environment, evaluation protocol, and extended analyses behind the main text. Specifically: Appendix lists the existing datasets we train on directly: HyDRA items and nine public text-toSQL datasets. Appendix details the SQL-originated construction: the shipped subsets, the SQL2S and S2SQL builds, corpus ingestion, and worked examples. Appendix details the search-originated construction: the seed pool and pipeline, the shipped databases, and worked examples. Appendix reports the SFT data ablation that adds each data family in turn. Appendix describes the local retrieval corpus that serves the web tools during trajectory generation, RL, and evaluation. Appendix describes the hybrid agent harness: its tool interface, episode execution, and comparison with other agent harnesses. Appendix gives the evaluation details for BrowseComp, BrowseComp-Plus, and Spider 2.0-lite, the inference configuration of every model, and the LLM judge prompts. Appendix analyzes the failures of the base, SFT, and RL models: the outcome of every rollout and commits justified by time, effort, or guess. Appendix gives the RL training parameters and an analysis of judge voting.

sections.title: B DIRECT TRAINING DATA
sections.content: We first include existing datasets that are used directly for training rather than as construction seeds. Specifically, we use 10,184 HyDRA items (Wu et al., 2026a) and 25,747 deduplicated text-to-SQL examples drawn from nine public datasets: Spider 1.0 (Yu et al., 2018), BIRD (Li et al., 2023), SynSQL (Li et al., 2025a), EHRSQL (Lee et al., 2022), LLMSQL (Pihulski et al., 2025), MMQA (Wu et al., 2025), LogicCat (Liutao et al., 2026), SParC (Yu et al., 2019b), and CoSQL (Yu et al., 2019a). These examples provide direct supervision for hybrid and SQL capabilities, respectively. We use random subset of SynSQL; for the other datasets, we keep only the questions for which at least one sampled trajectory is correct. Table 5 summarizes the composition. C.1 BUILDING SQL2S: THE BRIDGE IS AN OUTPUT CELL SQL-ORIG-SYN (synthetic split) runs all four steps below; SQL-ORIG-PRIM (primary split) is then refabricated by an anti-shortcut pass. An LLM judge scores each candidate on rarity, referent-collision risk, and whether credible document can mention it; candidates that are ambiguous or cannot host fabricated document are dropped. (ii) Hop One (Coined Facts): Each fact is built answer-first: the bridge is pinned from the gold SQL, fact about it (a business rule, data-dictionary definition, or specification value) is invented, and only then is the question written. Coined names are pronounceable pseudo-words made globally unique by reservation registry. Answers are NAME types (coined company org, coined team, coined person, coined product model, coined award) or VALUE (number). Questions may also define coined composite metric (name, abbreviation, description, and formula faithful to the gold SQL) in domain-knowledge block: 77.4% of SQL-ORIG-SYN and 14.0% of SQLORIG-PRIM questions have one. Only SQL-ORIG-SYN also serves these definitions through the knowledge-lookup tools  (Table 14)  , since the real databases behind SQL-ORIG-PRIM have no knowledge base. Each fact gets one gold document, which wraps the answer sentence in realistic body in register chosen by entity type (news or biography for people, press release or filing for organizations, spec page or review for products, internal wiki for private metrics); golds average 890924 characters, so most fit one retrieval chunk. Each fact also gets up to ten typed hard negatives, full-length perturbations of the golds answer sentence that each flip exactly one constraint  (Table 8)  . (iii) Hop Two (The Intersection Hub): Given coined facts about the bridge, hubs are minted over fact subsets: the gold hub satisfies all constraints, each near-miss hub satisfies 1, and each constraint is the missing one for some near-miss. The question refers to each fact by paraphrase, never verbatim. Each hub-affiliation gold names the hub exactly once, never in the first sentence and never as the sole anything, among at least two same-type distractors, and gets seven to ten near-miss negatives that never contain the hub name. From 3,389 entities with four or five coined facts each and three or four constraints per item, the build yields 15,421 items, with 61,732 hub golds against 432,044 hub negatives (1:7). 18 (iv) Verification: Six deterministic gates run first: (a) the fact is searchable in the gold; (b) the entity is present in the gold; (c) both fall inside one 300-character window; (d) the answer is not in the question; (e) the answer is not value in the seeds output column; (f) the constraint intersection is singleton. Five model-based gates follow: gold faithfulness, no-document parametric probe, mask test (with the gold removed, the fact must not be recoverable from the items negatives), negative-reader denoising (drop any negative that answers the question), and premise plausibility. Primary-split bridges can be famous real entities (e.g. Google Photos in Example 2), which invites early lock-on and distractor capture: committing to the first plausible candidate, or to retrieved near-miss, before every constraint is checked. Both failure modes are documented for long-horizon search agents (Sinha et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2025) and for LLMs reading noisy retrieved text (Shi et al., 2023; Cuconasu et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025b; Pham et al., 2026), and salient parametric prior makes lock-on worse (Xie et al., 2024). The pass keeps the seed SQL and refabricates the web puzzle with DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DeepSeekAI, 2026), which also samples the trajectories: parametric-prior decoy receives the longest and most authoritative document in the item (salience inversion), and real homonym of the bridge and at least two namesake or misspelling negatives are added. C.2 BUILDING S2SQL: THE ANCHOR IS WHERE-CLAUSE LITERAL SQL-ORIG-S2SQL-SYN is built from the synthetic split only, since few primary-split seeds pass the anchor gates. Gold documents, typed negatives, and verification follow steps (ii) and (iv) of Appendix C.1; Example 3 in Appendix C.4 walks through one item. (i) Anchor Selection: Candidates are string literals under EQ, IN, or LIKE nodes of the gold querys syntax tree, on name-bearing column (e.g. name, title, team, city, product) and outside an enum stop-set such as {active, yes, male}. The execution check replaces the predicate with tautology and requires the row set to change, which rejects co-filter decoys whose rows join key or threshold already pins; the membership gate requires the anchor to appear in the question but not in the output. Execution must also be non-degenerate (0 < rows < table), and the anchor must support at least three clues, which rejects famous anchors that single hop resolves (e.g. Canada). namability judge then rejects five recurring shapes: class labels (Sedan), status values (in progress), generic metrics and awards (Golden Globe), common personal names (Smith), and ambiguous acronyms or over-coarse places (USA). Anchors are not filtered for rarity, since difficulty comes from the clues and decoys. Seeds are instead chosen to cover every SQL group, the gold queries sharing one structural signature (table-count bucket, CTE depth, window-function class, and aggregate class, e.g. T5+CTE1WIN:rankAGG:none); the seed pool keeps all 2,518 groups. (ii) Relation Fan-out & Hub Construction: Each clue ties the anchor to coined entity through one of 31 relations over seven anchor types  (Table 9)  . Coined names are also 19 checked against the names already in the corpus, and name that still collides gets distinctive suffix. The anchor is the only entity that satisfies every clue, and each coined near-miss satisfies all but one, so an item carries about 43 hard negatives. The final question lists the clues first and the seed question last, with the anchor hidden; otherwise the model answers with the entity name instead of the result table. sections.title: F LOCAL CORPUS
sections.content: Generating teacher trajectories and RL rollouts against search API is costly at our scale, and results drift as the web changes. We therefore serve the agents web tools from local corpus of 21M documents, which combines real web text from the June 2026 English Wikipedia dump1 and subset of the CC-MAIN-2025-26 snapshot of FineWeb (Penedo et al., 2024), with the fabricated gold documents and hard negatives of Sec 3.2 (ingestion details in Appendix C.3). Our design goal is to reproduce the observations search API returns, so that the agents tool interface is unchanged when it moves to live search. In particular, such APIs return query-dependent snippets: each result shows the part of the page that best matches the query rather than fixed summary. To support it, we split each document into chunks by greedily packing whole sentences up to 500 characters, without overlap. Both documents and chunks are indexed for hybrid retrieval, which combines BM25 (Robertson & Zaragoza, 2009) with dense cosine similarity. web search retrieves in two stages. Document-level retrieval first selects 100 candidate documents. At the chunk level, the same hybrid index then retrieves pool of chunks from these candidates, and cross-encoder reranker (Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B; Zhang et al., 2025) reorders the pool. Each document is ranked by its highest-scoring chunk (MaxP; Dai & Callan, 2019), and the top 20 documents are returned, one result per page, each with its title, URL, date, and snippet taken from that chunk. visit web returns the full text of document, but only for URLs that appeared in an earlier search result, so the agent cannot fetch pages it has not found.

sections.title: G HYBRID AGENT HARNESS
sections.content: A question is only hybrid if solving it requires the agent to obtain evidence from both structured and unstructured sources. Our harness provides the common interaction protocol through which the agent accesses these sources. It is native tool-calling loop: the model takes turn, the requested tools are executed, their observations are appended to the context, and the process repeats until the agent commits an answer or exhausts its budget. Trajectories are kept in the models native tool-calling format rather than encoded into prompt text and parsed back out. The protocol seen during training is therefore the same one used when the model is served, and each rollout can be judged, replayed, and packed for supervised fine-tuning without format conversion. We use this harness for teacher trajectory collection, reinforcement-learning rollouts, and evaluation of our trained checkpoints. G.1 TOOL INTERFACE The agent is given neither the database schema nor any web document in its prompt, so both sources must be accessed through the tools in Table 14. On the database side, run sql is the only interface to the underlying SQLite database and supports both schema discovery and subsequent query execution. Three knowledge-lookup tools expose database-specific metrics and their definitions when needed. On the web side, web search returns ranked results with short snippets, while visit web retrieves the full text of selected document. The same interface supports both SQL2S and S2SQL: in SQL2S, SQL result provides the bridge entity for subsequent web research, whereas in S2SQL, an entity resolved from web evidence is used in the subsequent SQL query. The harness does not prescribe either ordering; the model selects its next tool from the same tool set at every turn. G.2 EPISODE EXECUTION Tool failures are returned to the model as ordinary observations rather than terminating the episode, allowing the agent to revise an invalid call or try different action. An episode ends when final answer succeeds, when model turn contains no tool call, or when the turn or wallclock budget is exhausted. As the remaining budget shrinks, the harness injects short reminder to stop exploring and commit an answer, specialized to the expected output type. For S2SQL, the agent submits an executable SQL query; for SQL2S and other text-answer tasks, it submits concise textual answer. 1https://dumps.wikimedia.org/enwiki/20260601/ 27 Table 14: Tools exposed by the hybrid agent harness. sections.title: H EVALUATION DETAILS
sections.content: This section details the evaluation protocol of 5: the two search-only benchmarks, the shared inference configuration, Spider 2.0-lite, and the judge prompts. HybridDeepResearch needs nothing beyond 5; every model is evaluated in the same SQL and retrieval environment. H.1 BROWSECOMP EVALUATION BrowseComp (Wei et al., 2025) is run against the live web, and the agent is equipped with five tools: web search: searches the live web; web fetch: retrieves the contents of selected webpage; pdf read: downloads and extracts text from PDF documents; read file: reads locally materialized files when needed; final answer: submits the final answer and terminates the episode. Web search. web search first queries the Brave Search API. If Brave returns no results, query containing multiple quoted spans is rewritten into an OR-style query and issued to Brave again. the search falls back to Serper (google.serper.dev), which returns Google search results. Tavily is not used in this evaluation. If the second Brave request also returns no results, Webpage retrieval. web fetch first attempts to retrieve webpage through Jina Reader (r.jina.ai) when Jina API key is available. If this fails, the page is fetched directly using local HTTP client and converted to text with MarkItDown. 28 PDF documents are handled by pdf read. The tool first downloads the PDF and attempts text extraction with pypdf; if this fails, it falls back to Jina Reader. The live-web environment requires BRAVE API KEY and SERPER API KEY; JINA API KEY is optional. API key values are neither stored nor reported. H.2 BROWSECOMP-PLUS EVALUATION The BrowseComp-Plus (Chen et al., 2026) corpus is indexed with the same hybrid retrieval backend as our local corpus. Retrieval operates directly over full documents; we do not use separate chunk index or local reranker. The agent is equipped with three tools: corpus search(query): performs semantic retrieval over the fixed corpus and returns the top five documents, including DOCID, URL, cosine score, and retrieval snippet; corpus fetch(docid): retrieves the full text of exactly one document identified by DOCID returned by corpus search; final answer: submits the final answer and terminates the episode. corpus fetch performs an exact lookup using the returned DOCID; it does not issue another semantic search and does not fetch the external webpage associated with the URL. sections.title: INFERENCE CONFIGURATION
sections.content: We use model-specific decoding settings while keeping the interaction budget fixed across model families unless otherwise noted. Qwen models. All Qwen models use maximum of 300 interaction turns, maximum of 32,768 generated tokens, and wall-clock timeout of 3,600 seconds. Decoding uses temperature 0.6, topp 0.95, and top-k 20. They are evaluated on 8 NVIDIA H200 GPUs, except on Spider 2.0-lite (Appendix H.4). GLM-5.2. GLM-5.2 uses maximum of 300 interaction turns, maximum of 65,536 generated tokens, and wall-clock timeout of 3,600 seconds. We set reasoning effort to max, temperature to 1.0, and top-p to 0.95. We do not explicitly set top-k. GLM-5.2 is evaluated on 8 NVIDIA B200 GPUs. Claude Sonnet 4.6. Claude Sonnet 4.6 uses maximum of 300 interaction turns, maximum of 32,768 generated tokens, and wall-clock timeout of 3,600 seconds. We set reasoning effort to medium. Other decoding parameters use the models default settings. H.4 SPIDER 2.0-LITE EVALUATION Spider 2.0-lite (Lei et al., 2025) contains 547 instances, of which 135 (local) are posed on SQLite databases distributed with the benchmark. The remaining 412 (bq, ga, sf, and sf bq) query cloud data warehouses and can only be executed through BigQuery or the benchmarks hosted Snowflake account. We use all 135 local instances, which span 30 databases, so the subset is determined by database engine alone and not by difficulty or results. Tools. The evaluation uses the agent harness of Appendix with web access removed and, unlike HybridDeepResearch, with the database schema given in the prompt. The agent is equipped with two tools: run sql(sql, description): executes one read-only query (SELECT, WITH, PRAGMA, or EXPLAIN) on the instances SQLite database and returns at most 500 rows, with 120-second limit per query; final answer(answer): submits the final answer and terminates the episode. 29 The system prompt lists only these two tools. call to any other tool returns an error message to the agent and does not end the episode. Prompt. The user message contains the question, the instances external-knowledge document if it has one, and the full database schema: the CREATE TABLE and CREATE VIEW statements of every table as stored in sqlite master, including column types and primaryand foreign-key constraints. No sample rows are included; the agent can inspect values with run sql. Thirteen of the 135 instances reference an external-knowledge document (eight distinct documents), which is inserted into the prompt verbatim. Final answer & graded query. The agent must submit, through final answer, the single query that answers the question in fenced sql block. If submission contains no SQL query, the harness rejects it and asks for the query, up to two times. The check is structural (a fenced sql block, SELECT . . . FROM, or WITH . . . AS (), so prose answer that merely contains the word select or with does not pass. We grade only the query submitted through final answer: the last fenced code block of its answer or, if it has none, the first SQL statement in it (SELECT . . . FROM or WITH . . . AS (), truncated at its first semicolon. Queries the agent ran with run sql are never graded. Judging. We use the official Spider 2.0-lite execution-accuracy metric. The submitted query is executed on the instances database, and its result is compared with the official gold execution results rather than with gold query, since only 24 of the 135 inthe official comparison (compare multi pandas table in stances ship one. We port spider2-lite/evaluation suite/evaluate.py) line by line. prediction is correct if it matches at least one of the instances acceptable gold results.A prediction matches gold result if every gold column, restricted to the instances condition cols when these are given, equals some column of the prediction. Row order is ignored, numbers are compared with an absolute tolerance of 0.01, missing values count as 0, and extra predicted columns are allowed. As in the official script, the predicted result is round-tripped through CSV before comparison. query that fails to execute is scored as incorrect. Execution limit. The official evaluator sets no execution limit for SQLite databases. We stop query after 600 seconds. To check that this limit does not affect any result, every query that reached it was re-executed with one-hour limit. Four submitted queries reached 600 seconds, two from the base model and two from the RL model; none of them finished within an hour, and they are scored as incorrect. Inference. The base model and the hybrid SFT and RL checkpoints are served in bf16 with vLLM 0.28 (Kwon et al., 2023) (maximum model length 262,144, prefix caching), with data parallelism 4 on four NVIDIA B200 GPUs. Decoding follows Appendix H.3 with thinking mode on. Because each instance requires committing single query rather than long-horizon research, we use 50 interaction turns and wall-clock timeout of 1,800 seconds per trajectory. H.5 LLM JUDGE PROMPTS Our HybridDeepResearch judges are adapted from the SimpleQA (Wei et al., 2024) judging format, with task-specific modifications for table-valued S2SQL outputs and textual SQL2S/Parallel outputs. BrowseComp and BrowseComp-Plus use the standard BrowseComp-style extracted-answer judging protocol without modification, so we do not reproduce that prompt here. S2SQL table judge. Your job is to look at question, gold SQL result table, and an agent SQL result table, and then assign grade of either ["CORRECT", "INCORRECT"]. The agent answered natural-language question by running SQL. Both tables below were produced by re-executing SQL on the same database: the gold table from the verified gold 30 SQL, and the agent table from the agent's SQL. Grade whether the agent table conveys the same answer as the gold table for the question, judged by meaning rather than exact table shape. Judge semantic equivalence: do not penalize purely presentational differences. Also note the following things: - First identify the key value(s) that answer the question: entities, counts, metrics, and any group or protocol average the question asked for. Judge those. Treat as presentational and do not penalize: column names, JSON key names, extra or missing nonessential columns, table shape, and row order when order was not asked for. - Row identifiers from different columns or namespaces are presentational when the askedfor metrics match. Different identifier strings alone do not make the table INCORRECT. Different metrics or different set of entities is INCORRECT. - Group labels may differ if each group's counts and metric lists still match. - Numbers match within small rounding margin. For percentiles and other window-function scores, difference of about 0.01 or less is CORRECT when the rest of the row matches. Extra or fewer decimals are CORRECT when they round to the gold at the gold's precision, or differ only by that window-function noise. shifted distribution or different entity or value is INCORRECT. - If the question asks for rank: the same entities in the same order are CORRECT even if one table uses global rank and the other ranks only inside the result set. different set of entities or different order is INCORRECT. - If the question asks for group or protocol average, or difference from such an average, that number is key value. It must match gold's grouping and scope. differently scoped average is INCORRECT even when the top entities and their raw scores match. - Grade INCORRECT when the agent table contradicts those key values, is empty or missing while gold is not, or buries the answer among many unrelated rows without isolating it. Here is new example. Simply reply with either CORRECT or INCORRECT. Don't apologize or correct yourself if there was mistake; we are just trying to grade the answer. ``` Question: {question} Gold table: {gold table} Agent table: {agent table} ``` Grade the agent table of this new question as one of: A: CORRECT B: INCORRECT Just return the letters "A" or "B", with no text around it. SQL2S and Parallel answer judge. Your job is to look at question, gold target, and predicted answer, and then assign grade of either ["CORRECT", "INCORRECT"]. It still identifies the same person as the gold target. ``` Question: What was the name of the UEFA club competition that ran from 1971 until it was rebranded in 2009? Gold target: UEFA Cup Predicted answer: UEFA Europa League (formerly the UEFA Cup) ``` This predicted answer is CORRECT because it names the same competition by its current official name and explicitly identifies the gold target as the former name. ``` Question: Which country is the origin of record CB752021? Gold target: Burundi Predicted answer: The country is Burundi. The top destination nations by reliability score from Burundi are: 1. Nicaragua 2. Fiji 3. Macao 4. Algeria Verification of clues: - Burundi is World Bank Group member. - Hafsa Mossi was Burundian politician and minister. ``` This predicted answer is also CORRECT because: - It clearly commits to the gold target as the answer to the question ("The country is Burundi"). - Extra supporting detail, explanations, verification, or related lists after the core answer are allowed and should not change the grade, as long as they do not contradict the gold target. The following are examples of INCORRECT predicted answers. ``` Question: What are the names of Barack Obama's children? Gold target: Malia and Sasha Predicted answer 1: Malia. Predicted answer 2: Malia, Sasha, and Susan. Predicted answer 3: Barack Obama does not have any children. Predicted answer 4: think it's either Malia and Sasha. Or it could be Malia and Jackie. Or it could be Joey and Malia. Predicted answer 5: While don't know their exact names, can tell you that Barack Obama has three children. Predicted answer 7: It may be the case that Obama's child is named James. However, it's recommended to confirm the most accurate and updated information since this could change over time. Gold target: Queens Predicted answer: Brooklyn ``` This predicted answer is INCORRECT because Brooklyn is different, nearby place not the same borough as the gold target. Also note the following things: - Grade based on whether the predicted answer correctly answers the question relative to the gold target. Focus on the committed core answer (often the first clear statement of the entity/value asked for). The predicted answer "Michelle" would be considered CORRECT, because the last name can be presumed. - Do not punish for typos in people's name if it's clearly the same name. - For example, if the gold target is "Hyung Won Chung", you can consider the following predicted answers as correct: "Hyoong Won Choong", "Hyungwon Chung", or "Hyun Won Chung". - Related is not the same. predicted answer that names different person, place, ethnic group, organization, work, or event from the gold target is INCORRECT, even if the two are nearby, historically linked, commonly confused, or belong to the same country, family , or category. - shortened, reordered, or unofficial form of the SAME proper name is CORRECT (dropping middle name, particle, or commonly omitted suffix still identifies the same person or entity). - former official name, current official name, or well-established alias of the SAME entity is CORRECT. Naming different entity, successor that is not the same thing, or merely related item is INCORRECT. Here is new example. Simply reply with either CORRECT or INCORRECT. Don't apologize or correct yourself if there was mistake; we are just trying to grade the answer. ``` Question: {question} Gold target: {target} Predicted answer: {predicted answer} ``` Grade the predicted answer of this new question as one of: A: CORRECT B: INCORRECT Just return the letters "A" or "B", with no text around it. 33 FAILURE ANALYSIS OF THE BASE, SFT, AND RL MODELS This section details the failure analysis behind 6.1. We analyze all 2,880 rollouts of the base, SFT, and RL models on the 120-question hard subset (3 models 120 questions 8 samples). The three models receive identical prompts, tool schemas, and decoding parameters (Appendix H.3), and rollout that ends without final answer call counts as wrong. Appendix I.1 assigns every rollout to exactly one outcome, and Appendix I.2 examines how the agents justify the answers they submit. Of the 120 questions, 35 are never solved by any of the three models (9 S2SQL, 21 SQL2S, and 5 Parallel). I.1 OUTCOME OF EVERY ROLLOUT Evidence tracing. We normalize strings by lowercasing them and removing accents and punctuation, and we count string as present in text when it matches on whole words. We trace two strings through every rollout, the bridge and the gold answer. For S2SQL, the bridge is the web-resolved entity (plus its database spelling when it differs); for SQL2S, it is the first cell of the gold SQL result. For Parallel, the SQL candidates are the rows of the gold SQL result, and the web candidates are the annotated search answers. string is surfaced if it appears in web search result or visited page, and in reasoning if it appears in the models reasoning. On S2SQL, the model uses the right entity if the bridge appears in its final text or submitted SQL. Paraphrases and entities encoded by ID do not match, so all evidence rates are lower bounds. Outcome categories. Each rollout receives the first category it matches, in this order. S2SQL: correct; no answer; prose answer without SQL; SQL fails to execute; wrong entity, with the right one never surfaced; wrong entity, with the right one surfaced; right entity with the wrong row count, the wrong columns, or wrong values. SQL2S: correct; no answer; bridge not retrieved by SQL; gold never surfaced; gold surfaced but never in reasoning; gold in reasoning but not answered. Parallel: correct; no answer; gold never in the SQL results; gold never on the web; gold in both sources, with the answer in the web candidates only, in the SQL candidates only, or in neither. S2SQL: wrong entity and wrong SQL. The base model usually fails before it builds query: 59.7% of its rollouts end without an answer, and 16.3% answer in prose without SQL. The trained models fail for two reasons of similar size. The first is resolving the wrong bridge entity (35.0% of SFT and 33.1% of RL rollouts), often plausible neighbor of the right one, such as Chad, Egypt, or Niger for Sudan, Pakistan for Chile, or Denmark for Iceland. In 13.8% and 15.6% of rollouts, the right entity does appear in search result or visited page, but the query is built on another one. When it appears only in visited page, it is usually passing mention in long page about something else, such as one row of table of countries. The second is building wrong SQL around the right entity (29.7% and 31.3%), most often with wrong values. Malformed SQL is rare: at most 4.1% of rollouts submit query that fails to execute. SQL2S: the search hop. The SQL hop succeeds: the bridge never appears in the SQL results in only 2.5% of SFT and 1.6% of RL rollouts. The search hop does not. For both trained models, the largest category is gold answer that never surfaces (52.2% of SFT and 52.8% of RL rollouts). Counting every category, the gold answer never appears in any search result or visited page in 59.4% and 54.1% of rollouts, and accuracy in those rollouts is at most 2.1%. When the gold answer does surface, the models often fail to use it: in 14.4% and 15.0% of rollouts it never enters the reasoning, and in 18.1% and 17.8% it enters the reasoning but different answer is submitted. Typical wrong answers are the bridge itself (about 7% of wrong SQL2S answers), salient entity next to the bridge (the capital Moroni for question whose bridge is the Comoros and whose answer is the village Iconi), and name copied from coined bridge (Jim Taylor for bridge named Taylortown). Parallel: coverage and the intersection. In 8.8% of SFT and 5.6% of RL rollouts, the answer is wrong and the gold answer never reaches the SQL results; in further 19.4% and 17.2%, it reaches the SQL results but never the web. The largest remaining failure is the intersection, which more rollouts reach as coverage improves: the gold answer appears in both sources, but the submitted answer is in only one candidate set (18.4% and 19.7%) or in neither (17.5% and 20.3%). sections.title: J RL TRAINING AND ANALYSIS
sections.content: J.1 RL TRAINING PARAMETERS RL training is conducted using framework built on PRIME-RL (Senghaas et al., 2025), with fully asynchronous training at asynchrony level 1, running on single 8-GPU node. We optimize GRPO objective (Shao et al., 2024) with standard-deviation-normalized advantages and promptlevel token-averaged loss, using CISPO (MiniMax et al., 2025) with importance weights clipped at 2.0 and negative-sample scale 1.0. We used AdamW (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019) with learning rate 1 106, ϵ = 1 1015, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.98, zero weight decay, and constant schedule without warmup. The reference-model KL penalty and explicit length penalty are disabled. Each step uses 32 prompts with group size 5. Rollouts use temperature 1.0, top-p = 1.0, up to 32k completion tokens per turn and max turns set to 100, with 128k token context limit. Inference uses vLLM (Kwon et al., 2023) with tensor parallelism 1 and 95% GPU memory utilization. We additionally perform group-level difficulty filtering for adapting dynamic policy. Groups with 0% or 100% solve rates are excluded from the main optimization stream because they provide little within-group reward contrast. task is removed from the training pool after being fully solved in = 1 consecutive rollout groups or failing completely in = 3 consecutive rollout groups. sections.content: As shown in Table 18, representative examples illustrate how five-vote majority judging resolves challenging cases involving semantic ambiguity and non-trivial variations in SQL result tables. Table 18: Representative cases where single-vote judging produces an incorrect reward while fivevote majority judging reaches the correct judgment. The SQL example illustrates that judging requires reasoning about result-level semantics rather than exact table matching. Case Example 1 Entity ambiguity. The reference entity is Charles Emmanuel III, while the model produces "Charles III". Although the two names are lexically similar, they refer to different monarchs. correct judgment therefore requires semantic entity resolution rather than string matching. Partial SQL correctness. The gold result filters to Fort de Pontisse, while the model recovers the same ranking but omits the final filter. Gold result Model result fort avg days held rank fort avg days rank Fort de Pontisse 6.0 Fort de Loncin Fort de Pontisse Fort de Fleron Fort de Flemalle Fort de Barchon 7.0 6.0 5.5 3.5 3.5 1 2 3 4 4 The model correctly computes the averages and ranking, and correctly places Fort de Pontisse at rank 2, but fails to apply the final filter. The final result is therefore incorrect despite substantial partial correctness, making the case difficult to judge reliably from surface-level table comparison.
